issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption covenant made in a partition agreement binds successors-in-interest when the agreement, read in context, shows no contrary intention and indicates that its benefits and burdens were intended to pass to them.
material_facts: A partition award between co-owners provided that either would give the other a preference before transferring any part of their share.

The award also provided for continuing rights and obligations concerning common passages, drainage, and other shared property, using the term “parties” in a way that included successors and assignees.
The pre-emption right was based on vicinage, and the agreement contained no indication that the parties intended the right to be personal or non-assignable.
The owners’ successors transferred the divided properties, and the later purchasers of the property subject to the covenant had notice of it.
The purchasers of the other share sued to enforce the pre-emption right against the later transferees.
issues.conclusion: The covenant was to be construed as binding on the original parties’ assignees and successors-in-interest and was enforceable against the transferees in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 23(b) and 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act and sections 37 and 40 of the Indian Contract Act, contractual rights and obligations ordinarily pass to representatives, assignees, and successors unless an express or implied contrary intention appears, subject to applicable exceptions. Section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act permits an obligation concerning land, though not an interest in land, to be enforced against a transferee with notice. The covenant’s wording and context—including the award’s treatment of continuing shared rights and the vicinage basis of pre-emption—showed that the parties intended it to bind successors. No earlier case was relied on as the basis for this conclusion.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_proceeding and preemption_covenant_in_partition_agreement and no_contrary_intention and context_indicates_successor_intent and transferee_has_notice

predicates.preemption_enforcement_proceeding: A claimant brings a proceeding to enforce a contractual right of pre-emption.
predicates.preemption_covenant_in_partition_agreeme: Co-owners agree as part of a property partition that one must give the other a preference before transferring the relevant property.
predicates.no_contrary_intention: The agreement contains no express or implied intention that the covenant is personal or does not pass to successors.
predicates.context_indicates_successor_intent: The agreement’s other terms or circumstances show that its continuing benefits and obligations were intended to extend to successors and assignees.
predicates.transferee_has_notice: The transferee of the property had notice of the covenant.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption covenant in a partition agreement contains no contrary intention, its context indicates that it extends to successors, and a transferee has notice, the covenant binds successors in an enforcement proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: The rule against perpetuities does not invalidate a contractual covenant of pre-emption that creates no interest in property, even when the agreement sets no time limit for exercising the right.
material_facts: The pre-emption covenant arose from an agreement made in connection with a partition of immovable property.
The covenant created a contractual option to pre-empt a transfer but did not itself create an interest in the property.
The agreement imposed no time limit within which the option had to be exercised.
The covenant was challenged as void under the rule against perpetuities.
issues.conclusion: The covenant did not offend the rule against perpetuities and was not void on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The rule against perpetuities concerns the creation of future interests in property, not contracts that create no such interest. Sections 14 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act establish that a contract for sale of immovable property does not, by itself, create an interest in that property; section 40 permits certain contractual obligations concerning land to be enforced against transferees with notice without treating them as interests in land. The Court relied on Walsh v. Secretary of State for India, South Eastern Railway Company v. Associated Portland Cement Manufacturers Ltd., and Witham v. Vane for the principle that personal contracts do not attract the rule; it distinguished the English approach in London and South Western Railway Company v. Gomm. It approved the approach in Ali Hossain Miya v. Raj Kumar Haldar, Aulad Ali v. Ali Athar, and Chinna Munuswami Nayudu v. Sagalaguna Nayudu, rather than the contrary earlier Indian decisions concerning agreements made before the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: perpetuity_challenge_to_preemption_covenant and contractual_preemption_option and covenant_creates_no_property_interest and no_exercise_time_limit

predicates.perpetuity_challenge_to_preemption_coven: A party challenges a pre-emption covenant as invalid under the rule against perpetuities.
predicates.contractual_preemption_option: The covenant gives a person a contractual right to pre-empt a transfer of property.
predicates.covenant_creates_no_property_interest: The covenant does not itself create an interest in the property.
predicates.no_exercise_time_limit: The agreement sets no time limit for exercising the pre-emption right.

issues.definition: If a contractual pre-emption option is challenged under the rule against perpetuities, creates no property interest, and has no time limit for exercise, the covenant is not invalidated by that rule.
